tagline.text: The highest peak in Mountain Province, reached through endless stone steps and mossy forest

location.label: Location

children.text: Mount Amuyao rises to about 2,702 m and is a well-known Cordillera peak climbed from the Barlig side of Mountain Province. You pass rice terraces, pine forest and mossy forest, and from the summit ridge you can see a sea of clouds and sunrise, but a guide is required and it takes a lot of stamina.

Mount Amuyao is a mountain in the Cordillera range of northern Philippines, and its widely quoted height is about 2,702 m. Some sources, such as PeakVisor, give 2,701 m, and older records even show 2,628 m, so the exact figure differs slightly by source. Administratively it straddles the border of Barlig in Mountain Province and Banaue in Ifugao, and it is described as the highest peak in Mountain Province. Broadcast relay antennas stand at the summit, and there is a small clearing where you can camp.

The mountain is famous for the scenery that is so typical of the Cordillera. Near the start, the rice terraces of the Awa area spread out, and as you climb you pass through a pine-lined ridge and then a thick, misty forest covered in moss. Much of the ascent is stone and earth steps, which has earned it the nickname of an endless staircase. On a clear day you can see Mount Pulag and the Kalinga mountain ranges from the top, and in winter you can hope for a sea of clouds spread out below your feet.

There are two main ways up. One is the Barlig backtrail, which climbs from Sitio Macalana on the Barlig side, and the other is the traverse from Barlig over the summit and down to Batad. According to the latest guidance, the traverse is open only with permission from the local tourism offices and through accredited operators, and individuals cannot simply walk it on their own. The most realistic choice is a two-day round trip on the Barlig backtrail.

The difficulty is described as about 6 out of 9 in dry weather and about 8 out of 9 when it is wet or cold. The climb to the summit usually takes 5–8 hours and the descent 4–5 hours. A day-hike round trip is possible but takes 9–13 hours, and one guide does not recommend it for most hikers. The usual plan is to sleep near the summit and watch the sunrise at dawn. The same guides say that on a clear day you can see Mount Pulag, Mount Napulauan and the Kalinga ranges from the top, and that pink Melastoma flowers bloom in summer. For safety, bring a rain jacket and spare clothes even in the dry season.

blocks.title: Awa rice terraces and the trailhead

children.text: The hike starts at Sitio Macalana at about 1,300 m. You walk through the rice terraces of Awa from the very beginning, so you enjoy the Cordillera farm landscape before you even start climbing toward the summit.

blocks.title: Pine ridge, Mount Alemmona and Mount Polis

children.text: After the rice terraces you climb a pine-forest ridge near Mount Alemmona and Mount Polis. The trees give shade from the sun, but the slope stays steady and your energy drains quickly.

As the elevation rises, you enter a misty forest covered in moss. Mobile signal drops out in this section, and it is known to get slippery in the rain, with leeches. There is said to be a spring on the way where you can get water, so ask your guide where it is.

blocks.title: Summit ridge sunrise and sea of clouds

children.text: From the summit ridge you can see the early-morning sunrise and a sea of clouds, and the best chance is said to be December–February. On clear days Mount Pulag, Mount Napulauan and the Kalinga ranges come into view.
Near the summit there is a bunkhouse where you pay about ₱100 to stay, and you can also pitch a tent in the clearing beside the antennas. It is first come, first served, so bring small bills.

The best months for hiking are November through May, and in December–February in particular there are many clear days, with a good chance of sunrise and a sea of clouds. In exchange, the summit temperature drops to 0–5℃ in this period, so warm gear is a must.

June–October is the rainy season, with typhoons and the damp southwest monsoon, and the trail turns to mud and leeches are reported, so it is best avoided. Landslides and rockfall can also block the road between Bontoc and Barlig. Even in the dry season, camping at the summit requires warm gear.

Barlig town has homestays costing about
a night. Meals are usually paluto, which means ordering in advance and having the host cook, at about

a meal. Guides note that Barlig is cash only and has no ATM, so withdraw enough in Manila or Bontoc. Landslides are frequent on the road between Bontoc and Barlig, so travel in daylight whenever possible.
Near the summit you can choose between the bunkhouse (about

) and camping in a tent. Water is said to be available from a spring about halfway up and from a stream near the end of the mossy forest, but carry at least 2 liters for the first stretch of steps and treat water before you drink it.
You must register at the Barlig tourism office, which is open weekdays
. Guides are limited, so book weeks ahead for weekends and holidays.
A doctor's certificate saying you are fit for climbing and strenuous activity is reportedly required. A general health certificate may not be accepted, so ask in advance.
One guide covers up to five hikers. From the sixth hiker you pay ₱100 per person extra or hire a second guide.
With so many steps, trekking poles and knee supports help.
There are fines for plastic bags, disposable bottles and polystyrene containers. Carry all your trash back down.
Signal is weak on the lower slopes and drops out in the mossy forest. Download offline maps in your map app.
Bring plenty of small bills. Change is hard to come by at the summit bunkhouse and the homestays.
Nearby sights include Lake Tufob,
20–30 minutes

2 hours
away.
Water can reportedly be refilled only at the spring partway up and the stream at the end of the mossy forest. Carry at least 2 liters for the first stretch.
A headlamp and spare batteries are essential. If your descent runs late, you will walk through the dark mossy forest.
Climbing without an accredited guide can lead to expulsion and fines, and the Batad traverse is open only through accredited operators.
Summit temperatures at night can fall close to 0℃. Bring warm clothing, gloves and a sleeping bag.
The rainy season brings landslides, rockfall, leeches and mud, which makes it dangerous. Postpone your trip if a typhoon is forecast.
There are sacred sites, so follow your guide's rules. Shouting, drinking alcohol on the trail, collecting orchids and disturbing wildlife are prohibited.
A day round trip is recommended only for very fit hikers. Be down before dark.
In an emergency you would contact the local disaster response office through the Barlig tourism office or your guide. Hospitals are on the Bontoc side, so check your insurance.
